results.result: Prior work established the basic framework of 30S ribosome assembly, including the structure of the 70S ribosome, the ability to reconstitute 30S subunits in vitro, and the hierarchical order and dependencies of r-protein binding under equilibrium conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 are all supported by established literature citations (Traub and Nomura 1969; Mizushima and Nomura 1970; Held et al. 1973, 1974; Stern et al. 1989). These represent well-established prior knowledge that provides the foundation for the current study.

results.result: Prior studies revealed that 30S assembly can proceed through multiple parallel pathways despite r-protein binding dependencies, and that misfolded rRNA structures lead to stable kinetic traps during in vitro reconstitution.
results.evaluation: Claims C6 and C7 are supported by multiple citations to prior work (Adilakshmi et al. 2008; Ridgeway et al. 2012; Kim et al. 2014; Talkington et al. 2005; Bunner et al. 2010a; Mulder et al. 2010; Sykes and Williamson 2009). These establish important context for understanding assembly complexity.

results.result: Assembly factors including RimM, RbfA, RimP, Era, RsgA, and KsgA have been implicated in various aspects of 30S assembly in vivo, though the precise role of RimP within the assembly factor network was previously unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C11 are supported by citations to prior work (Wilson and Nierhaus 2007; Shajani et al. 2011; Williamson 2003; Clatterbuck Soper et al. 2013; Datta et al. 2007; Jomaa et al. 2011b; Sharma et al. 2005; Guo et al. 2011; Boehringer et al. 2012; Nord et al. 2009; Bunner et al. 2010b). This establishes the motivation for investigating RimP's role.

results.result: Recent methodological advances in quantitative mass spectrometry and automated electron microscopy enable high-throughput analysis of heterogeneous ribosome assembly intermediates.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C15 are supported by citations to prior methodological work (Charollais et al. 2003; Chen and Williamson 2013; Clatterbuck Soper et al. 2013; Guo et al. 2013; Leong et al. 2013; Suloway et al. 2005; Lander et al. 2009; Radermacher et al. 1987; Yoshioka et al. 2007; Voss et al. 2010). This establishes the technical foundation for the hybrid approach.

results.result: Five distinct groups of 30S assembly intermediates were identified in WT E. coli by combined qMS and EM analysis, representing a progression from early intermediates lacking the head domain (Group I) through intermediates with unanchored (Group II) or partially docked heads (Group III) to late intermediates and mature subunits (Groups IV and V).
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C22 are directly supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1C-D and 2A-H, combining qMS measurements of r-protein abundance with EM structural analysis. The classification into five groups is based on both compositional and conformational differences observed across multiple fractions. The data are internally consistent between qMS and EM observations.

results.result: The central pseudoknot appears to be formed in Group III but unformed in Group II particles, with the detachment of the head from the platform in Group II suggesting unstable or unformed central PK regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C23 and C24 are supported by structural observations from EM data (Figures 2B-C) showing distinct head positioning between Groups II and III. The inference about central PK status is reasonable based on the known structural role of the central PK in anchoring the head domain, though this is an inference from structural data rather than direct measurement.

results.result: Deletion of RimP has a stronger effect on central PK exposure than deletion of RimM or RbfA, as measured by RNase H accessibility assays, and correlates with increased abundance of Group II particles with unanchored heads.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 are supported by RNase H assay data (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-C) and EM analysis (Figure 3C-D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) comparing multiple deletion strains. The correlation between RNase H cleavage and Group II particle abundance across strains provides strong support for the connection between RimP and central PK stability.

results.result: The ΔrimP strain shows altered ribosome profiles with increased 30S/50S and decreased 70S particles compared to WT, and qMS analysis reveals that S2, S3, S12, and S21 are specifically depleted in ΔrimP relative to WT.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30 are supported by sucrose gradient data (Figure 4A) and qMS data (Figure 4C). The sucrose gradient result is consistent with prior work (Nord et al. 2009). The specific depletion pattern of S2, S3, S12, and S21 is clearly shown in the hierarchical clustering analysis.

results.result: Pulse-labeling experiments demonstrate that ΔrimP intermediates are on-pathway, eventually maturing into 70S ribosomes, but with delayed incorporation of S12 and late-binding proteins S2, S21, and S3. Early-binding proteins like S4 have large precursor pool sizes while depleted proteins like S12 have negligible pools.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C38 are supported by pulse-labeling qMS data (Figure 4D-F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C). The higher fraction labeled values in 30S particles compared to 70S ribosomes (C31) demonstrate that intermediates are on-pathway. The precursor pool size analysis (C34-C35) and kinetic modeling (Figure 4E) provide quantitative support for delayed incorporation of specific proteins. The clustering of S12 with late binders despite being an early binder in WT (C36) is a key finding supported by the data.

results.result: Group II intermediates are dramatically enriched (>3-fold) in ΔrimP samples compared to WT.
results.evaluation: Claims C39 and C40 are supported by direct comparison of EM data between WT and ΔrimP strains (Figures 1D, 5B-C). The >3-fold enrichment is quantified in Figure 5C using a combined dataset approach that allows direct comparison.

results.result: Group II particles exhibit highly variable head domain positioning constrained by a flexible linker (likely 16S residues 910-919), and may contain a nearly complete complement of head domain r-proteins, indicating that head domain assembly can occur prior to central PK formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C45 are supported by EM analysis including 2D class averages, 3D RCT volumes, variance analysis (Figure 5D-F), and Maskiton analysis (Video 2). The inference about the flexible linker (C43) is reasonable based on the structural context and observed range of motion. The conclusion that head domain assembly can precede central PK formation (C45) is a significant finding supported by the structural data showing assembled heads with unformed central PK.

results.result: Affinity-purified ΔrimP intermediates with unstable central PK show severe depletion of S2 and S12, partial depletion of S3 and S5, but high abundance of most other 3′-domain r-proteins, suggesting head domain formation is not perturbed until very late stages of assembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 are supported by qMS analysis of affinity-purified intermediates (Figure 6A). The specific depletion pattern and the inference about head domain assembly timing (C48) are reasonable based on the uniform abundance of most 3′-domain proteins. However, the affinity purification method may introduce some bias toward certain intermediate types.

results.result: Cryo-EM structures of Group I intermediates lack the entire 3′-domain including helix 27, and clearly lack density for S5 and S12. Variability between Group I structures arises mainly from differences in the platform region, suggesting that platform stability may depend on 3′-domain assembly and docking.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C54 are supported by cryo-EM data (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C) and codimensional PCA analysis (Figure 6D). The lack of density for specific structural elements and proteins is clearly demonstrated. The inference about platform stability depending on 3′-domain assembly (C54) is reasonable based on the observed variability pattern, though this remains a hypothesis requiring further testing.

results.result: The central pseudoknot is essential for translation and conserved across all kingdoms of life. The yeast ribosomal biogenesis factor Mrd1 was previously implicated in central PK formation and binds to 18S rRNA helices h27 and h28 adjacent to the central PK.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 are supported by citations to prior work (Brink et al. 1993; Poot et al. 1998; Segerstolpe et al. 2013). This establishes important evolutionary and functional context for understanding the significance of central PK formation and provides a precedent for assembly factors acting on this structure.

results.result: RimP is composed of two RNA-binding domains and may play an analogous role to Mrd1 in binding to 16S rRNA regions adjacent to the central PK.
results.evaluation: Claim C59 about RimP structure is supported by established knowledge. However, claim C60 is explicitly speculative, based on structural similarity between RimP and Mrd1. While the speculation is reasonable given the experimental results showing RimP's role in central PK formation, direct evidence for RimP binding to specific rRNA regions is not provided in this study.

results.result: The authors propose that RimP acts during early and late stages of 30S biogenesis to stabilize the central pseudoknot, allowing subsequent incorporation of central-PK binding r-proteins S5 and S12 and late-binding r-proteins S2, S3, and S21.
results.evaluation: Claims C61 and C62 represent the authors' proposed model based on their experimental data. While explicitly presented as a proposal, the model is well-supported by the combined evidence from RNase H assays, EM structural analysis, qMS protein composition data, and pulse-labeling kinetics. The model integrates multiple lines of evidence showing RimP's effect on central PK stability and the delayed incorporation of specific proteins in ΔrimP.

results.result: The authors propose a model where premature central PK formation is blocked by the 5′-leader structure, RbfA promotes h1 formation and may act synergistically with RimP to stabilize the central PK, while RimM acts independently to facilitate head domain assembly. RimP may be one of the earliest factors to act on the assembling 30S subunit.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C67 represent a proposed mechanistic model integrating RimP with other assembly factors. While C63 is established knowledge and C66-C67 are reasonable inferences from the data showing different intermediate distributions in ΔrimM vs ΔrimP, claims C64-C65 about RbfA acting synergistically with RimP are explicitly speculative and not directly tested in this study. The model is plausible but requires additional experimental validation.

results.result: RimP has previously been shown to accelerate S5 and S12 binding in vitro, and the authors suggest that adding RimP to in vitro reconstitution experiments may help promote central PK formation and avoid kinetically unfavorable Group I and II intermediates.
results.evaluation: Claim C68 is supported by citation to prior work (Bunner et al. 2010b). Claim C69 is a reasonable suggestion based on integrating the prior in vitro results with the current in vivo findings, though it remains a prediction requiring experimental validation. The suggestion is well-grounded in the data showing RimP's role in central PK formation.

results.result: Previous in vitro reconstitution studies showed Group I-like and Group II-like intermediates at early time points, with their abundance subsiding upon S5 and S12 incorporation, consistent with the current in vivo observations that pre-central PK conformations are viable on-pathway intermediates.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C73 are supported by citations to prior work (Mulder et al. 2010) and represent a synthesis of prior in vitro observations with the current in vivo findings. The consistency between in vitro and in vivo observations strengthens the interpretation that Group I and II intermediates represent kinetically unfavorable but on-pathway states.

results.result: RimP has been shown to bind free 30S subunits but not 70S ribosomes, indicating direct interaction with 30S assembly intermediates.
results.evaluation: Claims C74 and C75 are supported by citation to prior work (Nord et al. 2009). The inference that RimP directly interacts with assembly intermediates (C75) is reasonable based on the binding specificity, though the exact binding site and mechanism remain to be determined.

results.result: The combined EM/qMS approach should have broad applicability to studying other ribosome assembly factors and macromolecular assembly processes in bacteria and eukaryotes.
results.evaluation: Claim C76 is a reasonable speculation about the broader applicability of the methodology. The successful application of the hybrid approach to characterize heterogeneous ribosome assembly intermediates demonstrates its potential utility for other complex assembly processes, though actual application to other systems would require validation.
